\chapter{Four Colors}
\label{ch:ur-colors}
\hlchaptermodality{13}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name red, white, black and blue in Urdu, and tell which colors change their ending for the noun they describe and which never do.}

Say all four colors — \ur{لال}, \ur{سفید}, \ur{کالا}, \ur{نیلا} — sorting the two that agree with the noun's gender from the two that never change, and trace \ur{نیلا}'s cousin nīlī forward through Persian and Arabic into English aniline.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[lāl]{\ur{لال} — \textquotedblleft{}red,\textquotedblright{} and a word that never changes shape}

\label{lesson:UR-C13-lal}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{\ur{روٹی}} — bread, an honest dead end with no English cousin. This lesson opens a new kind of word: colors, starting with the one you'd use for a ripe tomato or a bride's dress.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{لال}} — \emph{lāl} — \textbf{red}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میرا} \ur{کوٹ} \ur{لال} \ur{ہے۔}} — \emph{merā koṭ lāl hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}My coat is red.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a color that never agrees}]
\textbf{\ur{لال}} ends in a consonant, not in \textbf{\ur{ا}}. That matters: it stays \textbf{\ur{لال}} whether the thing it describes is masculine or feminine, singular or plural. \emph{merā kamīz lāl hai}, \emph{merī ṭopī lāl hai} — same word, no change. Not every color in this book will be this simple.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{لال}} is borrowed from Classical Persian \textbf{\ur{لَال}}, \textquotedblleft{}red.\textquotedblright{} No further ancestor is documented for the Persian word itself — the trail simply stops, the same honest kind of dead end \textbf{\ur{روٹی}}'s Sanskrit root hit last lesson, except this time on the Persian side of the book's two layers rather than the inherited one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{lāl} — red; then \textbf{merā koṭ lāl hai}
  \item \emph{Note:} \textbf{\ur{لال}} never changes its ending, unlike the colors still to come
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{lāl} $\leftarrow$ Persian, no further root — like \textbf{\ur{روٹی}}'s Sanskrit root, but on the other side of the book's two layers
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ur{لال}} mean, and which layer does it belong to — inherited or Persian? (\textbf{Red}; \textbf{Persian}.) Does \textbf{\ur{لال}} change its ending for a feminine noun? (\textbf{No — it stays \ur{لال}.}) Does \textbf{\ur{لال}} have a documented ancestor before Persian? (\textbf{No — an honest dead end.}) Is \textbf{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ}} written as one word or two in Urdu spelling? (\textbf{Two, spaced — unlike Persian's joined form.}) When you read \textbf{\ur{میرا} \ur{نام} ... \ur{ہے}} right to left, does the spoken order of the words change? (\textbf{No — the script direction changes, the spoken order does not.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%84\%D8\%A7\%D9\%84}{Wiktionary: \ur{لال}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[safed]{\ur{سفید} — \textquotedblleft{}white,\textquotedblright{} and English joins the family this time}

\label{lesson:UR-C13-safed}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{\ur{لال}} — red, Persian, and a dead end. This word is also Persian, also ends in a consonant, and also never changes shape. But its root does not stop where \textbf{\ur{لال}}'s did.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{سفید}} — \emph{safed} — \textbf{white}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میری} \ur{ٹوپی} \ur{سفید} \ur{ہے۔}} — \emph{merī ṭopī safed hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}My cap is white.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Like \textbf{\ur{لال}}, \textbf{\ur{سفید}} never changes its ending.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{سفید}} continues Middle Persian \emph{spēt}, from Old Iranian \textbf{*spaita-}, from Proto-Indo-Iranian \textbf{*ćwaytás}, from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*\'{k}weyt-}, \textquotedblleft{}to shine, white.\textquotedblright{} That is the \textbf{exact same root} behind Sanskrit \textbf{śvetá}, \textquotedblleft{}white\textquotedblright{} — so \textbf{\ur{سفید}} and Sanskrit's word for white split at the Indo-Iranian fork, one road east into Sanskrit, one road west into Iranian and then Urdu, the same shape as \textbf{\ur{دل}} and \emph{hṛdaya} two chapters back.

This time a third road leads somewhere new: that same PIE root, through Proto-Germanic, gives English \textbf{white} as well. \textbf{\ur{پوچھنا}} and \emph{porsīdan} were cousins by two roads; \textbf{\ur{سفید}}, \textbf{śvetá}, and \textbf{white} are cousins by three.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{safed} — white; then \textbf{merī ṭopī safed hai}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{\ur{لال}} — Persian, dead end; \textbf{\ur{سفید}} — Persian, and the root keeps going
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{safed} $\leftarrow$ Middle Persian $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*\'{k}weyt-} $\to$ Sanskrit \textbf{śvetá} $\to$ English \textbf{white}
  \item \emph{Say it:} one root, three roads this time, not two
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ur{سفید}} mean? (\textbf{White}.) Name its two settled cousins in other languages. (\textbf{Sanskrit śvetá; English white.}) Recall \textbf{\ur{ٹھیک}} and how a short Urdu word once bridged to a Hindi cognate — how is that bridge different from what \textbf{\ur{سفید}} just did? (\textbf{\ur{ٹھیک}}'s bridge was Urdu-to-Hindi, the same modern language pair; \textbf{\ur{سفید}}'s is a PIE root three languages deep.) How did the earlier take-leave dialogue end? (\textbf{With \ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ}, spoken by both voices.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%B3\%D9\%81\%DB\%8C\%D8\%AF}{Wiktionary: \ur{سفید}}, \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/white}{Wiktionary: white}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kālā]{\ur{کالا} — \textquotedblleft{}black,\textquotedblright{} and the first color that agrees}

\label{lesson:UR-C13-kala}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{\ur{سفید}} — white, cousin of Sanskrit \emph{śvetá} and English \textbf{white}, three roads from one PIE root. This word is inherited rather than Persian, and it breaks the \textquotedblleft{}never changes\textquotedblright{} rule the last two colors kept.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کالا}} — \emph{kālā} — \textbf{black}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میرا} \ur{کوٹ} \ur{کالا} \ur{ہے۔}} — \emph{merā koṭ kālā hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}My coat is black.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میری} \ur{ٹوپی} \ur{کالی} \ur{ہے۔}} — \emph{merī ṭopī kālī hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}My cap is black.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a color that agrees like \ur{مِیرا}}]
\textbf{\ur{کالا}} ends in \textbf{\ur{ا}} — and a color ending in \textbf{\ur{ا}} changes with the noun it describes, exactly the way \textbf{merā}/\textbf{merī} changed for gender back in the family chapter. Masculine stays \textbf{\ur{کالا}}; feminine becomes \textbf{\ur{کالی}}. \textbf{\ur{لال}} and \textbf{\ur{سفید}} never had to make this choice, because neither one ends in \textbf{\ur{ا}}. Watch for it again on the last color of this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{کالا}} is inherited from Sanskrit \emph{kāla}, \textquotedblleft{}black, dark\textquotedblright{} — so far, the same kind of story as \textbf{\ur{بھائی}} or \textbf{\ur{آنکھ}}. But \textbf{\ur{کالا}}'s root does not continue into Proto-Indo-European at all. It is usually traced instead to Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*kār-}, \textquotedblleft{}black, to be burnt\textquotedblright{}: Sanskrit itself borrowed this color word from its Dravidian neighbours, long before any of it reached Urdu. Inherited from Sanskrit, yes — but Sanskrit's own source sits outside the Indo-European family this book has been tracing.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{kālā} — black, masculine; \textbf{kālī} — black, feminine
  \item \emph{Choose:} \textbf{merā koṭ kālā hai} against \textbf{merī ṭopī kālī hai}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{\ur{سفید}} never changes; \textbf{\ur{کالا}} always agrees
  \item \emph{Name:} \textbf{\ur{کالا}}'s root sits outside Indo-European, in Dravidian — unlike every other inherited word so far
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ur{کالا}} mean, and what does it become before a feminine noun? (\textbf{Black}; \textbf{kālī}.) Is \textbf{\ur{کالا}}'s ultimate root Indo-European? (\textbf{No — Proto-Dravidian, borrowed into Sanskrit.}) Which two colors so far never change their ending? (\textbf{\ur{لال} and \ur{سفید}.}) Does \textbf{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ}} need a verb or an agreement ending to work as a farewell? (\textbf{No — speakers use the fixed formula simply as \textquotedblleft{}goodbye,\textquotedblright{} no conjugation required.}) When choosing \textbf{kaise} or \textbf{kaisī}, whose gender decides the choice — yours, or the person you're addressing? (\textbf{The person you're addressing.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%DA\%A9\%D8\%A7\%D9\%84\%D8\%A7}{Wiktionary: \ur{کالا}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nīlā]{\ur{نیلا} — \textquotedblleft{}blue,\textquotedblright{} and this book's fourth color closes the set}

\label{lesson:UR-C13-nila}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{\ur{کالا}}/\textbf{\ur{کالی}}, the color that agrees, against \textbf{\ur{لال}}, the color that never does. This chapter's last word decides which kind it is, then does something none of the other three managed: it left Urdu again, centuries later, and became an English word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{نیلا}} — \emph{nīlā} — \textbf{blue}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میرا} \ur{کوٹ} \ur{نیلا} \ur{ہے۔}} — \emph{merā koṭ nīlā hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}My coat is blue.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{نیلا}} ends in \textbf{\ur{ا}}, so it agrees exactly like \textbf{\ur{کالا}}: feminine \textbf{\ur{نیلی}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{نیلا}} comes from Sanskrit \emph{nīla}, \textquotedblleft{}dark blue.\textquotedblright{} No further root is documented behind it — an honest dead end backward, unlike \textbf{\ur{کالا}}'s root, which kept going sideways into Dravidian.

But Sanskrit's related word \textbf{nīlī}, \textquotedblleft{}the indigo plant,\textquotedblright{} did not stop there. It travelled forward: into Persian \textbf{nīla}, then Arabic \textbf{an-nīl} (\textquotedblleft{}the indigo\textquotedblright{}), then Portuguese \textbf{anil}, and finally into English as \textbf{aniline}, the name nineteenth-century chemists gave the dye compound first found in indigo. \textbf{\ur{سفید}} reached English through a shared PIE root, inherited by both languages independently. \textbf{\ur{نیلا}}'s route to English is a completely different shape: one word, borrowed forward through four languages, arriving in English only a couple of centuries ago.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{nīlā} — blue, masculine; \textbf{nīlī} — blue, feminine
  \item \emph{Sort:} agrees — \textbf{\ur{کالا}, \ur{نیلا}}; never changes — \textbf{\ur{لال}, \ur{سفید}}
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{nīlā}'s cousin \textbf{nīlī} $\to$ Persian $\to$ Arabic \textbf{an-nīl} $\to$ Portuguese \textbf{anil} $\to$ English \textbf{aniline}
  \item \emph{Say it:} all four colors — \textbf{\ur{لال}, \ur{سفید}, \ur{کالا}, \ur{نیلا}} — with \textbf{\ur{کوٹ}} or \textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two of this chapter's four colors agree with the noun they describe, and which two never change? (\textbf{Agree: \ur{کالا}, \ur{نیلا}. Never change: \ur{لال}, \ur{سفید}.}) What English word ultimately comes from the same root as \textbf{\ur{نیلا}}'s cousin \textbf{nīlī}? (\textbf{Aniline.}) Recall the phrase that closed a first introduction with a pleased response — say it now. (\textbf{\ur{آپ} \ur{سے} \ur{مل} \ur{کر} \ur{خوشی} \ur{ہوئی}.}) Does Urdu spell \textbf{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ}} joined, the way Persian does, or spaced? (\textbf{Spaced.}) Reading \textbf{\ur{میرا} \ur{نام} ... \ur{ہے}} right to left changes which direction — the script's, or the spoken word order's? (\textbf{Only the script's.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%86\%DB\%8C\%D9\%84\%D8\%A7}{Wiktionary: \ur{نیلا}}, \href{https://www.etymonline.com/word/aniline}{Etymonline: aniline}.
\end{tcolorbox}
